analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Dodd-Frank rules that oversee risky giant financial firms and let the government wind them down.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it had no cosponsors and sat in four House committees until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase Title I of the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, which created the Financial Stability Oversight Council — a panel of regulators that identifies financial firms whose collapse could shake the whole economy and subjects them to tougher oversight. It would also erase Title II, which gives the government authority to take over and wind down a failing giant financial firm in an orderly way, instead of letting it collapse chaotically or be rescued with taxpayer money. The bill would then restore the laws in place before Dodd-Frank, as if those protections had never existed. It never advanced past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the largest banks and other giant financial firms would benefit most. Repealing Title I ends the process that designates certain firms as systemically important and puts them under stricter capital and supervision requirements. Repealing Title II ends the government's power to resolve a failing giant firm without a bankruptcy that can freeze credit markets. Firms would gain freedom from the toughest parts of the post-2008 oversight regime.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The largest banks and financial firms

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Title I of Dodd-Frank, which created the Financial Stability Oversight Council that identifies and tightens oversight of firms whose failure could threaten the financial system.
Repeals Title II of Dodd-Frank, which gave the government orderly liquidation authority to wind down a failing systemically important financial firm without a chaotic bankruptcy.
Restores the laws that existed before those titles, as if Dodd-Frank Titles I and II had never been enacted.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, ordinary households would bear the risk side of the bargain. Without Title I, risky firms would escape the heightened scrutiny meant to catch danger before a crisis; without Title II, the failure of a giant firm would fall back into bankruptcy or a bailout, and the costs of a breakdown — lost jobs, frozen credit, taxpayer exposure — would land on the public, as happened in 2008.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and households exposed to crises

drawbacks.text: Critics of repeal point out that Title II's orderly liquidation authority is the mechanism designed to prevent the pattern of 2008, when a giant firm's failure (Lehman Brothers) froze credit markets and forced emergency government interventions that used taxpayer money.

Supporters of repeal argued in good faith that Title II gives the government broad discretion over failing firms and could turn into a bailout vehicle, reviving the problem of rescuing creditors of failed companies with public funds; this was the strongest case for the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit would flow almost entirely to the largest financial firms, which would shed the strictest post-2008 oversight. The cost is concentrated in the loss of the two tools Congress built specifically to prevent another 2008-style collapse: early identification of systemically risky firms, and a way to wind one down without a market panic. Even the honest argument for the bill — that resolution authority could be abused as a bailout — accepts that some mechanism for handling a giant firm's failure is needed; this bill offers none. On balance the cost to the public outweighs the gain to firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees, moved only to a subcommittee, and was never reported out or brought to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lynn Westmoreland (R-GA) introduced the bill in the House on April 29, 2015.
The House referred it to four committees: Financial Services, Agriculture, Judiciary, and Ways and Means.
On May 27, 2015 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit within the Financial Services Committee.
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary households and taxpayers kept the Dodd-Frank protections the bill would have removed — the council that flags systemically risky firms and the authority to wind down a failing giant firm without a bailout. The largest financial firms never gained the repeal they would have needed to shed that oversight.

for.name: Rep. Lynn Westmoreland
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Dodd-Frank Titles I and II.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral; never reported the bill or scheduled action
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee for the remainder of the 114th Congress, taking no action beyond a subcommittee referral, so it never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Only one Republican sponsored the bill and no one cosponsored it, so the record shows a single sponsor rather than a party-wide effort either for or against.

industries.industry: Largest banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: Repealing Title I and II would free the biggest firms from Financial Stability Oversight Council designation and the orderly liquidation regime, the strictest post-2008 rules. The gain comes from shedding oversight whose purpose is protecting households from the fallout of a financial crisis.

industries.industry: Nonbank systemically important financial firms (insurers and others designated under Title I)
industries.note: Firms like big insurers were designated for heightened Fed supervision under Title I; repeal would erase that designation process entirely. Their gain is escape from scrutiny, at the public's risk.
